scenes.text: Your phone is charging on the nightstand. Now follow that cable backward. Into the wall, out to the street, up the power lines, and keep going.
For about 18 percent of America's utility-scale electricity, the Energy Information Administration says, this trip starts with a split atom.

Today we follow that energy the whole way. And two things on this trip might surprise you. Roughly two-thirds of the energy never leaves the power plant as electricity. And the electrons at the plant never reach your phone.
Here's the idea: your phone charger is the last link in a long chain of handoffs. Each step turns the energy into a form the next one can use.

Inside a reactor, the fuel is uranium, formed into small ceramic pellets. The EIA says each pellet holds about as much energy as 150 gallons of oil. The pellets are stacked end to end in fuel rods 12 feet long.

When a uranium-235 atom absorbs a slow-moving neutron, it splits into two smaller atoms. That's fission. It releases a lot of energy, plus extra neutrons that can split more atoms, which keeps a chain reaction going. The plant uses the heat from all that splitting to boil water.
As of March 2026, the U.S. had 94 operating commercial reactors at 54 plants in 28 states, according to the EIA.
scenes.graphic: stat tiles: 94 reactors / 54 plants / 28 states (EIA, as of March 2026) + 91% average capacity factor in 2025 (EIA)

scenes.text: And they run hard. In 2025, the average U.S. nuclear plant produced 91 percent of its maximum possible output. The EIA calls that the capacity factor, and nuclear's was higher than any other type of power plant.

Next, heat has to become motion. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission says only two reactor types make commercial power in the U.S., and about two-thirds of the licensed reactors are pressurized water reactors.
In those, water under high pressure carries heat from the core to a steam generator, where it boils water in a separate loop. The other type, a boiling water reactor, makes steam right in the core.
Either way, the steam is piped to a turbine and spins it. The turbine drives a generator, where a spinning magnet induces current in coils of wire. That's where motion finally becomes electricity.
The generator doesn't spin at just any speed. In North America, the grid runs on alternating current at a standard 60 hertz, meaning 60 cycles every second, and the generators run in sync with it.
And here's the first big loss. The EIA tracks how much heat a plant uses for each kilowatt-hour it sends out. For U.S. nuclear plants in 2025, that works out to an efficiency of about 33 percent.
scenes.graphic: bar: of 100 units of reactor heat, ~33 become electricity, ~67 do not (from EIA 2025 nuclear heat rate 10,443 Btu/kWh; 3,412 / 10,443 = 32.7%)

scenes.text: So roughly two-thirds of the heat never becomes electricity. The used steam is cooled back into water in a condenser, and that leftover heat has to go somewhere. Some plants use cooling towers. Others use a lake, a river, or the ocean.
That's not unique to nuclear. Coal plants also run on steam, and in 2025 their average efficiency was about the same, around 32 percent.
According to the Department of Energy, generators usually put out electricity at 5,000 to 34,500 volts. Think of voltage as electrical pressure, the push behind the flow of current.
Right at the plant, a step-up transformer raises that pressure for the long haul. Typical U.S. transmission lines run at 138,000, 230,000, 345,000, 500,000, or 765,000 volts.
scenes.graphic: voltage ladder diagram: generator 5-34.5 kV -> step-up transformer -> transmission 138 / 230 / 345 / 500 / 765 kV (DOE 2015) -> substation -> distribution (e.g. 7.2 kV) -> pole transformer -> home 120/240 V -> charger -> low-voltage DC

scenes.text: Why push the voltage that high? A transformer can't create power. So when it raises the voltage, the current drops by the same factor.
And the energy a wire loses as heat depends on the square of the current. Cut the current in half, and that loss drops to a quarter. That's why the grid goes high.
scenes.graphic: diagram: same power, voltage x2 -> current x1/2 -> wire heat loss x1/4 (loss proportional to current squared; HyperPhysics)

scenes.text: Or in the EIA's words, higher voltage makes long-distance transmission more efficient and less expensive.
But you can't plug a lamp into 345,000 volts. So the way back down starts at a substation, where transformers lower the voltage for local lines.
In one Department of Energy example, a substation takes power in at 34,000 volts and sends it out at 7,200 volts on neighborhood distribution lines.
The final step-down happens close to your home: the can-shaped transformer on a utility pole, or a box on a concrete pad where the lines run underground.

It feeds a standard U.S. house two 120-volt hot wires plus a neutral. One of them gives you the 120 volts at a regular outlet. Both together give you 240 volts for big loads like a clothes dryer or an electric range.
scenes.graphic: diagram: pole transformer with center tap -> hot wire A 120 V, neutral, hot wire B 120 V; A to neutral = 120 V outlet, A to B = 240 V dryer/range (HyperPhysics)

scenes.text: Along that whole route, some energy is lost on the way. The EIA estimates that transmission and distribution losses averaged about 5 percent from 2018 through 2022. So the big loss happens back at the plant. The grid itself is fairly thrifty.
scenes.graphic: bar: of electricity sent out on the grid, ~95% delivered, ~5% lost in transmission and distribution (EIA, average 2018-2022)

scenes.text: Now for the second surprise. We say electricity flows, so it's easy to picture electrons racing from the plant to your house. They don't.

In a copper wire, the average drift of electrons is only fractions of a millimeter per second, according to physics notes from Georgia State University. In one of their examples, it's less than a third of a millimeter per second.
scenes.graphic: log-scale comparison: electron drift ~0.00028 m/s (HyperPhysics copper-wire example) vs. signal along a wire ~300,000,000 m/s (speed of light)

scenes.text: And on our grid, they don't even drift one way. With alternating current, the voltage swings positive, then negative, and back, 60 times every second. So the current keeps reversing, and the electrons mostly shuffle back and forth in place.
scenes.graphic: sine wave: household AC, 120 V effective, peaks +170 V / -170 V, 60 cycles per second (OpenStax College Physics 2e)

scenes.text: Transformers break the chain, too. Inside one, energy crosses from one coil of wire to another through a magnetic field in an iron core.

So what makes the trip? The energy. Push on one end of the line, and the push travels. Georgia State's notes put it this way: it's the change, the signal, that moves along wires close to the speed of light. Across a hundred miles, that's under a thousandth of a second.

Which brings us back to the little box on your nightstand. Federal rules actually define it: an external power supply converts household electric current into DC current, or lower-voltage AC, to run a product.

A battery charges when current is pushed through it one way, and wall current flips direction 120 times a second. So the charger lowers the voltage and turns AC into direct current, which flows in one direction.

Then comes the final handoff. As the Department of Energy puts it, electricity has to be converted into chemical potential energy before it can be readily stored. While charging, electrons move through the circuit and ions move through the battery, and the energy ends up held in chemistry.
And that's the end of the trip. Energy from a split uranium atom, now waiting as chemistry in your pocket.

Quick recap. Fission makes heat. Heat makes steam. Steam spins a turbine, and the turbine drives a generator that makes 60-hertz power. In 2025, only about a third of a nuclear plant's heat became electricity.
scenes.graphic: flow diagram of the trip: fission -> heat -> steam -> turbine -> generator (60 Hz) -> step-up transformer -> transmission -> substation -> distribution -> pole transformer -> 120/240 V outlet -> charger (AC to DC) -> battery chemistry; labels '~1/3 of heat becomes electricity (2025)' and '~5% lost on the grid (2018-2022)'

scenes.text: Transformers push the voltage up to hundreds of thousands of volts so the long trip loses less, then step it back down to 120 and 240 volts at your house. The electrons mostly stay put; the energy makes the trip.
Here's my question for you: which step surprised you most? The heat that never becomes electricity, or the electrons that never leave your walls? Tell me in the comments.
If you like seeing the hidden machinery behind everyday life, subscribe to Other End of the Wire. Every source behind the numbers in this video is in the description. Follow the electron.

meta.description:
Plug in your phone, then follow the cable back: through the wall, down the street, up the power lines, all the way to a nuclear reactor.
Step by step, we trace every handoff, where energy gets lost, and why the electrons themselves never make the trip.

In this video:
- Fission, fuel pellets, and how a reactor makes heat
- Steam, turbines, and a generator locked to 60 hertz
- Why about two-thirds of a nuclear plant's heat never becomes electricity
- The voltage ladder: why transmission lines run at hundreds of thousands of volts
- Substations, pole transformers, and the 120/240-volt setup in U.S. homes
- How much is lost on the grid (about 5%)
- Electron drift vs. the speed of the energy
- What your phone charger actually does
